title: Lead Inspection Checklist for OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1025 Lead Exposure
subtitle: Use on walk-throughs of general industry lead work areas, after process changes and before the annual review of the compliance program.
instructions: Mark every item OK, Defect or N/A, and note the area, date and inspector.
For each Defect, record what was found, who will correct it and by when, then recheck the item once it is fixed.
Manufacturer's instructions for respirators, ventilation and vacuums, and your site rules, may add checks to this list.

sections.title: Exposure assessment and monitoring
items: An initial determination covers each workplace or operation with lead and states whether anyone may be exposed at or above the action level of 30 µg/m³.
If the determination was negative, a written record shows the basis, date, worksite location and employees monitored.
Personal samples run 7 or more continuous hours, with one or more per shift for every job classification and work area.
Monitoring between action level and PEL
Exposures at or above the action level but below the PEL are re-sampled at 6-month intervals or more often.
Results above 50 µg/m³ are followed by quarterly monitoring.
Each production, process, control or personnel change that may add lead exposure since the last sampling was followed by additional monitoring.
Each affected employee received results in writing or by posting within 15 working days of the employer receiving them.
Written notices for results over the PEL say the PEL was exceeded and describe the corrective action taken or planned.

Records list sample dates, number, duration, location and results, methods with evidence of accuracy, any respirators worn, names and job classifications of employees monitored and represented, and environmental variables.

sections.title: Controls, ventilation and respirators
items: The written program describes each lead-emitting operation, the chosen controls, technology considered, monitoring data on emission sources and an implementation schedule.
The written program shows a revision within the last 12 months.
A copy is kept at the worksite and can be examined and copied by affected employees and their representatives.
Capture velocity, duct velocity or static pressure readings are logged at least every 3 months and within 5 days of any production, process or control change.
Any recirculating exhaust has a high efficiency filter, a back-up filter, and working lead monitoring with automatic bypass.
Where rotation is used, the schedule lists each employee's name or ID number, time spent and exposure levels at each job or station.
A respiratory protection program meeting 1910.134 covers every employee required to wear a respirator.
Every powered and non-powered air-purifying respirator in use has HEPA filters.
Full facepiece respirators, not half masks, are worn where lead aerosols irritate eyes or skin.
An employee who asks for a respirator is given one.

sections.title: Protective clothing and housekeeping
items: Employees over the PEL or at risk of irritation to skin or eyes wear coveralls, gloves, hats, shoes or shoe covers and eye or face protection, issued free.
Clean, dry clothing is issued at least weekly, and daily to anyone whose exposure, without regard to respirators, is over 200 µg/m³ as an 8-hour TWA.
Used clothing goes into closed containers in the change room.
Bags and containers of contaminated clothing carry the full DANGER label wording set out in the standard.
Whoever cleans or launders the clothing has been told in writing about lead's harmful effects.
No one blows, shakes or otherwise dusts off clothing or equipment.
Floors, ledges and equipment show no lead dust buildup that could practicably be removed.
No compressed air is used to clean floors or surfaces where lead collects.
Sweeping, shoveling or brushing is used only where vacuuming or an equally effective method was tried and failed.
Vacuums are used and emptied in a way that minimises lead dust returning to the work area.

sections.title: Hygiene facilities
items: No food, drinks, tobacco products or cosmetic use in above-PEL areas outside change rooms, lunchrooms and showers.
Clean change rooms are provided for employees working where airborne exposure is above the PEL, without regard to respirators.
Change rooms have separate storage for protective clothing and equipment and for street clothes that prevents cross-contamination.
Employees working over the PEL shower at the end of the shift.
No one required to shower leaves wearing shift clothing or equipment.
The lunchroom has a temperature-controlled, positive-pressure, filtered air supply and is readily accessible.
Employees wash hands and face before eating, drinking, smoking or applying cosmetics.
Protective clothing brought into the lunchroom has had surface lead dust removed by vacuuming, downdraft booth or other cleaning.

sections.title: Medical surveillance, training and signs
items: Everyone who is or may be exposed at or above the action level for more than 30 days per year is enrolled in medical surveillance.
Each covered employee has been offered blood lead and ZPP testing no less often than every 6 months.
Employees whose last result was at or over 40 µg/100 g are retested at least every two months.
No employee whose periodic and follow-up tests both showed at least 60 µg/100 g remains in work with lead exposure at or above the action level.
Each examined employee has a copy of every examining or consulting physician's written opinion.
Employees in any area with potential airborne lead exposure have been told what the two appendices (A and B) contain.
Each employee in the training program has been trained within the past 12 months.
Containers of lead are labelled and employees can reach the safety data sheets.
Required DANGER lead signs are posted at every work area where the PEL is exceeded.
Signs are lit and clean so the legend is readily visible.

references: 29 CFR 1910.1025: Lead (Part 1910 Subpart Z, Toxic and Hazardous Substances)
